Shinjuku Station East Exit

Kabukicho Crossing

name: Harajuku Station (JJK)

description: The museum inspired the bathhouse in Spirited Away.

name: Adachi City (Shoplifters)
description: The film captures the quieter, more suburban neighborhoods of Tokyo.

name: Tokyo Station (First Ward)
description:
The 1st Ward is where the CCG Main Office is located, and it serves as the headquarters for anti-Ghoul operations. It’s based on Chiyoda, home to major governmental buildings and Tokyo Station.
Notable Spot: Tokyo Station, a historic station with modern vibes, representing the CCG's power and influence.

name: Roppongi (3rd Ward)
description:
Description: The 3rd Ward features Roppongi, a famous nightlife district and key location in Tokyo Ghoul where Kaneki and Rize go on their fateful date.
Notable Spot: Roppongi Hills, known for its luxury shopping and skyline views, including a perfect view of Tokyo Tower at night.

name: Tokyo Skytree (6th Ward)
description:
Description: In Tokyo Ghoul, the 6th Ward is known for its high-tech vibe, which is mirrored by Taitō’s Tokyo Skytree, the tallest tower in Japan, representing a modern and futuristic Tokyo.
Notable Spot: Tokyo Skytree — a great spot for viewing Tokyo’s cityscape and tying in the "Neo-Tokyo" feel.

name: Tokyo Metropolitan Government Building (JJK)
description: Description: This towering building, located in Shinjuku, appears in Jujutsu Kaisen and is an iconic structure in Tokyo. It’s featured when major city-wide incidents unfold in the series.

name: Aoyama Cemetery (JJK)
description: Description: This location serves as the setting for darker moments in Jujutsu Kaisen. Aoyama Cemetery, known for its peaceful setting amidst the city, provides the backdrop for eerie scenes in the show.

name: Senkaku Junction (JJK)
description: Description: The multi-level highway junction is used for intense fight sequences in Jujutsu Kaisen. Its twisting roads provide a unique urban battle setting.

name: Yoyogi National Gymnasium (JJK)
description: Description: This landmark appears during the events of the series, representing a key battle arena.

name: Hotel Gajoen Tokyo (Sprited Away)
description: Hotel Gajoen in Tokyo is believed to have inspired the design of the bathhouse in Spirited Away. Known as one of Tokyo's "Museum Hotels," the hotel features stunning, traditional Japanese architecture with lavish interior designs, ornate rooms, and unique artistic displays, closely resembling the detailed design of the bathhouse in the film.

name: NTV Big Clock designed by Hayao Miyazaki
description: Description: A giant mechanical clock designed by Hayao Miyazaki himself, this Ghibli-themed clock is located outside Nippon Television Tower in Shiodome. Every hour, the clock comes alive with a whimsical performance.

name: Suga Shrine (Your Name)
description: The staircase where the characters meet in Your Name is located near Suga Shrine in Yotsuya, Tokyo. This spot has become a pilgrimage site for fans of the movie.

name: Asukayama Park (Spirited Away)
description: Old anime style yellow bus that can be used for scene recreations.

name: Tamagawa Aqueduct Greenway (Garden of Words)
description: Scene: The shaded pathways of the Tamagawa Aqueduct serve as the setting for reflective walks in The Garden of Words.

name: Nakano Broadway (Steins;gate)
description: Scene Description: Nakano Broadway is a hidden gem often featured for its retro shops and otaku culture. In Steins;Gate, it reflects the world of collectors and enthusiasts.

name: Bar Benfiddich
description: Located in Shinjuku, this speakeasy is known for its unique cocktails made using herbs and spices sourced from around the world.

name: Gen Yamamoto
description: This elegant speakeasy in Azabu-Juban is all about the art of the cocktail. Each drink is crafted with precision and care using only the freshest ingredients.

name: Rooftop Bar Andaz Tokyo Toranomon Hills
APOLLO BAR GINZA
description: Incredible whiskey selection, and a very gracious host. Don’t expect much English (you are in Japan, so you should not expect it), and like all small specialty bars, there is a small cover charge; however the host is gracious and we spent hours speaking about samurai films, whiskey, and music. Did I mention the whiskey selection is amazing?

name: Sawanoi - Ozawa brewery
description: Great spot for a quiet day in Ome. Easy walk from Sawai Station and right on the river, so you actually get scenery while you drink. The tastings are cheap and good, and you keep the little cup. Tours fill up fast and are only in Japanese, but the staff is helpful and the whole place is relaxed. If you’re already doing the valley or the river walk, stopping here is worth it.

name: BAR Willow's
description: Incredibly attentive bartender with clear, careful English and a real sense of hospitality. This has become a regular stop for me in Tokyo and I end up here multiple times every trip. Quiet, small, and easy to relax in, even though it sits above a row of louder bars. Cocktails are precise, the Moscow mule and martini in particular, and the light food works well if you stay for a few rounds. There is a table charge and you pay for hand–carved ice and mineral water, but the prices make sense for the level of service. If you want a calm bar where you are actually looked after, this is worth paying for.

name: 98wines Winery
description: Established 2016 by Yuki Hirayama, former sake brewer who retrained in Burgundy. The "98" refers to the year he began winemaking experiments, not the founding date. The winery occupies a converted 1970s agricultural warehouse. Koshu grapes are grown on pergola trellises at 400m elevation, traditional Yamanashi method that reduces fungal pressure in humid summers. Natural wine production means ambient yeast fermentation, no filtration, minimal sulfur. Annual production: 8,000 bottles. Tastings by appointment Tuesday-Sunday. Hirayama speaks functional English and French.

name: A-FACTORY
description: Waterfront commercial facility opened 2011. Apple cider brewery (Aomori produces 50% of Japan's apples). 15 restaurants and shops. Bay views from second floor. Located next to Wa Rasse. Open 09:00-20:00. Free entry.

name: Benitsuru
description: FLUFFY Pancakes—a pancake shop that perfectly balances salt and sweetness in its pancakes, making it a representative sweets store for those sightseeing in Asakusa.

name: Kanda Yabu Soba
description: a favorite of mine; a soba restaurant renowned for its traditional Edo-style noodles. The restaurant, rebuilt following a fire, continues to serve various soba dishes, including the Kamo-san ban soba featuring thick slices of duck and the ten-seiro soba paired with crispy shrimp.

name: KEY'S CAFÉ 秋葉原SEEKBASE店
description: A coffee shop within walking distance in Akihabara with wifi and good group seating. Open early and is a good place to study.

name: Himuka Shokudo
description:
Shokudo (食堂, shokudō) are casual restaurants or cafeterias that serve a variety of inexpensive Japanese dishes. Many of them are mom-and-pop, hole-in-the-wall type restaurants where the locals eat. They are numerous across Japan in urban centers and on the countryside. 

A meal at a shokudo usually cost around 800 to 1500 yen.

name: Suzukien Asakusa
description: the world's richest matcha gelato with seven intensity levels, catering to matcha newcomers and aficionados. Established through a collaboration between Suzukien, a historic tea shop from 1853, and Nanaya, a matcha sweets factory, this venue is a must-visit for its unique range of matcha gelato flavors.

name: Tesshin
description: teppanyaki, particularly featuring premium Kuroge Wagyu beef. Their signature dish is the Kuroge Wagyu Steak, priced at 1,380 JPY plus tax, seasoned with salt, kombu, and wasabi, offering a quintessential Japanese flavor profile.

name: Yakiniku King
description: A top-rated all-you-can-eat Yakiniku restaurant in Tokyo, Yakiniku King specializes in Japanese BBQ and offers a wide selection of meats for grilling. It's known for its quality, variety, and value, making it a must-visit for meat lovers. In 2022, it beat other well-known chains like Gyu-Kaku to rank as the number one Yakiniku spot. The restaurant also caters to tourists with English touchscreen menus.

name: Fruits Parlor Gotō
description: —café with sweet fruit parfaits near the old Hanayashiki amusement park. The menu, which changes seasonally, features delights such as grape and melon parfaits during summer, alongside other sweets like pancakes, kakigori shaved ice, and ice cream. It's a perfect spot for those seeking seasonal fruit desserts.

name: Buta-Daigaku Shimbashi
description: —Known for its pork bowls, which cost approximately 600 Yen for a small size, this is a must-visit for savory pork bowl lovers. It is located near Shibuya.

name: Ginza Kagari - Soba
description: — (Prepare to wait) famous for its sophisticated take on chicken ramen. The restaurant's signature dish, tori-paitan, features a creamy, rich broth derived from chicken, which provides a velvety texture and deep flavor.

name: Hobo Shinjuku Norengai
description: located a short 6-minute walk from Odakyu Shinjuku Station or Minami-Shinjuku Station, offers a collection of restaurants housed in traditional Japanese houses. This area provides a more classic and atmospheric dining experience compared to the modern establishments around Shinjuku Station. The term "Noren-gai" translates to "shop curtain town close to Shinjuku," referring to the traditional curtain (noren) that signifies an open shop. These 8 renovated old folk houses host a variety of dining options, not limited to Japanese cuisine.

name: Soba House Konjiki-Hototogisu
description: —(Prepare to wait) a ramen restaurant in Shinjuku, Tokyo, celebrated for its unique and sophisticated flavors. Awarded a Michelin star in 2018, this ramen establishment is renowned for its shoyu soba.

name: Ramen Sugimoto
description: —(Prepare to wait) ramen shop located in Nakano, Tokyo. This shop offers a unique ramen experience that both locals and visitors highly praise. The restaurant is known for its special shio (salt) ramen, which includes a generous topping of chashu pork, a perfectly cooked egg, and homemade wontons.

name: Shiro-Hige’s Cream Puff Factory
description: Nestled in Setagaya, this unique spot Offers Totoro-shaped cream puffs starting at 400 Yen. It is also a spot for Studio Ghibli fans and sweet tooth indulgers.

name: Hakushū Teppanyaki
description: This establishment shines with its premium Japanese Wagyu Beef prepared teppanyaki-style in Shibuya. It is celebrated for top-notch Kobe beef.

name: Kicks Cafe&Bar
description: A great local place to get a burger.

name: YAKITORI Nonotori Nihonbashi
description: Yakitori Nonotori in Nihonbashi offers an exceptional dining experience, particularly through its Premium Omakase Course, which features seasonal, expertly grilled skewers and side dishes. The restaurant is praised for its use of binchotan charcoal, which imparts a unique flavor to the yakitori, and its signature tamago kake gohan (rice with eggs cooked in an earthenware pot). Many diners appreciate the combination of traditional techniques with creative, modern twists, along with the attentive service. For a full experience, the omakase paired with sake or wine is highly recommended.

name: Hinoya Curry Akihabara
description: A good introduction to Japanese curry; it is a little spicy.

name: HIGUMA Doughnuts
description: HIGUMA Doughnuts in Tokyo Dome City offers fluffy, delicious donuts that are highly praised for their light texture and gentle sweetness.

name: Kantan-na Yume
description: Kantan-na Yume feels like a hidden gem tucked away in a quiet part of the city. When I visited, the peaceful atmosphere struck me right away—a nice change from Shibuya just minutes away. The wagashi I tried were exquisite, beautifully made, and paired perfectly with a cup of matcha.

name: Homemade Ramen 麦苗
description: f you're looking for an outstanding ramen experience, I highly recommend Homemade Ramen 麦苗. I visited recently, and despite not typically favoring shoyu broths, their version completely won me over with its depth and rich umami flavor. The noodles and toppings were exceptional—the steak in the deluxe toppings was some of the best I've had. Do note that you'll need to arrive early, around 9 or 10 AM, to put your name on the list due to its popularity. But trust me, the wait is worth it.

name: Gonpachi
description: 'KILL BILL: VOLUME I' (2003) - The inspiration for the 'House of Blue Leaves'

name: Yumune Chaya
description: Boil some eggs and sweet potatoes in the public hot spring – best bought at Yumune Chaya, the teahouse adjacent to the Yumune Kusushi Tōkō-ji Temple (squeezed between the river and the public onsen) – they make great provisions for your hike.

name: Sansaro Cafe
description: Sansaro Café & Guesthouse is a quiet and friendly stop along the Kumano route. The rooms are simple and clean, and the setting above the river is peaceful. There is no bath in the house, but the free ticket to Satsuki Onsen works well and is an easy walk. Supper and breakfast are cooked with care and fit the homestay feel. The owner is warm, helpful, and creates a comfortable atmosphere without trying too hard.

name: Masahiko Ozumi Paris
description: Masahiko Ozumi Paris really lives up to its reputation for cakes that look like works of art. Each one is intricate, creative, and surprisingly delicious — not just pretty for photos. The flavors are refined, balanced, and not overly sweet, which I really appreciated.

name: Rikuro’s Namba Main Branch
description: Rikuro’s cheesecake is absolutely worth trying once — soft, jiggly, and more eggy and airy than the dense Western style. The raisins on the bottom aren’t for everyone, but they add a touch of sweetness that grew on me. The real drawback is the line: it moves slowly, and since they only sell whole cakes, it’s a commitment (especially for solo travelers).

name: Honke Owariya Main Branch
description:
Visiting Japan’s “oldest soba restaurant” is more about the experience than just the food. The building and atmosphere are beautiful — traditional, calm, and steeped in history — and that’s something you can’t get just anywhere. Service was polite and efficient, even with the crowds.

As for the soba: it was good, but not mind-blowing.

name: TENYU kyoto 天佑（てんゆう）京都
JOJOPUB
description: A hidden gem by Kyoto Station! By day, the spice curry lunch is rich, balanced, and full of variety — the three-curry plate is a must. At night, it turns into a cozy bar with great drinks, friendly staff, and a relaxed vibe. Perfect for either a hearty meal or a few quiet cocktails.

name: Milky Way
description: Stopped in after walking around the lake and the place really does feel like someone’s grandmother opened her living room to the public. Two older ladies run everything themselves and they are genuinely kind. The food is simple, homemade, and better than it looks. I would get the curry. It is the kind of mild, comforting Japanese curry that tastes like it has been made the same way for decades. Portions are modest but clean and satisfying. Cash only and no toilet inside, but it is a quiet, warm stop if you want a break from the tourist crowds.

name: Fuso Ann
description:
t’s tiny (just around 10 seats), run by one incredibly kind woman who cooks, serves, and welcomes you all at once. The menu is very limited — basically soba noodles and a handful of traditional desserts — but everything is fresh, simple, and prepared with real care.

The soba is comforting, light, and perfect after a walk by the lake. The desserts, especially the matcha mochi and anmitsu.

name: Gyoza no Umechan
description: This little family-run spot in Nikko is the kind of restaurant you hope to stumble across while traveling. The menu is small and straightforward — ramen, curry, rice bowls, and of course their famous gyoza — but everything feels homemade and cooked with care. The gyoza are huge, juicy, and easily the standout dish, while the ramen has that warm, comforting “home kitchen” flavor you don’t get from chain shops.

name: Isshiki SAKANA HIROBA
description:
Isshiki Sakana Hiroba is the kind of market that shows you exactly what the local coast pulls in without dressing it up. Stalls are lined with fresh fish, dried seafood, and snacks, and the vendors are quick with samples even if communication stays simple. It is busy, loud, and direct in a way that feels honest rather than chaotic.

The real highlight is eating upstairs or at the small counters. Unagi, kaisendon, grilled seafood, and fried items are all straightforward and fresh.

name: Kanetaya
description:
Kanetaya is a long-running seafood restaurant with two different dining spaces on the same property. One side functions as a more formal Japanese dining room. The other operates like a casual restaurant with donburi, set meals, and hitsumabushi style dishes. Both sides use fish sourced from Choshi, and freshness is the dominant reason people go.

The menu tilts heavily toward raw fish, sardine dishes, eel, and mixed seafood bowls, plus seasonal items like oysters and bamboo shoots.

name: Cafe Bocu
description:
Cafe Bocu sits just off the Kumano Kodo, tucked far enough into the trees that you start wondering if you missed the turn. It feels like someone’s countryside home that happens to serve lunch to the few people who know it exists. The room is quiet, the air smells like baking bread, and the view is nothing but green.

Food here is simple and careful. Light vegetable-forward plates, fresh bread coming out of the oven, the kind of lunch that feels clean and handmade rather than heavy.

name: iro
description: Really nice café along the river near Waseda with a quiet, relaxed vibe. The tea menu is excellent and the toast is solid, especially for a simple breakfast or afternoon break. It can fill up, and seating is compact, but the atmosphere makes it worth the effort. Service is consistently kind.

name: Karashibi Miso Ramen Kikanbō Kanda Honten
description:
—(Prepare to wait) popular for its intensely spicy Karashibi Miso Ramen. The interior, characterized by its black paint, taiko music, and festival-style devil masks, adds to the immersive dining experience. You can customize their spice level on a scale of five for both "kara" (chili heat) and "Shibi" (numbing spice from sansho pepper mix), catering to varying spice tolerances.
1. Feel free to challenge my “Oni” title; we can sit side by side if you live that spicy life. 😉

name: Udatsu Sushi
description:
Udatsu delivers the full package without a single wasted gesture. The service is precise, quiet, and attentive in the way the best Tokyo counters are, and the presentation is meticulous without ever feeling staged. Every piece was balanced, clean, and confidently prepared. The pairings, both sake and the small seasonal touches, were thoughtful rather than showy, and the pacing of the course made the meal feel effortless.

I have eaten a lot of sushi across Japan, and this is easily among the best I have had. Nothing here feels gimmicked or inflated. It is the craft itself, executed at an exceptionally high level. It is hard to imagine anyone walking away disappointed with this standard of work.

Reservation required.

name: Tenryuji Temple Shigetsu
description:
The vegan set lunch at Tenryū-ji was beautifully balanced, seasonal, and surprisingly filling without ever feeling heavy. Every dish had subtle, layered flavors that showed real care in preparation.

The setting makes it unforgettable: sitting in view of the temple gardens and koi pond, the atmosphere is serene and quiet, adding to the sense that you’re eating something more meaningful than just food. Service was kind and efficient, though very little English is spoken, so patience and openness go a long way.

name: LATTE ART MANIA TOKYO
description: If you're looking for a cool, creative coffee spot, Latte Art Mania is definitely worth a visit. I appreciated the attention to detail in their intricate latte designs. The space is small, but the energy is inviting, and the charcoal latte offers something unique—both in flavor and presentation.

name: Yakumo Saryō
description: This serene and minimalist setting for a traditional Japanese breakfast was designed by the renowned architect Shinichiro Ogata. It provides a genuine cultural experience through its dining, highlighting Japanese cuisine as an art form involving various cultural elements, from the dishware to the chef’s etiquette. Yakumo Saryo offers a traditional Japanese breakfast called "Asacha," focusing on tea, priced at ¥4,000 (around $37).

name: tonkatsu.jp Omotesando
description:
This place is doing something very deliberate with breed, fat, and fry, and the results make sense on the plate. The cut I chose was cooked to a precise medium, juicy without feeling heavy, and the crust was clean, crisp, and even.

Get a reservation.

name: Saijoen
description: Saijoen feels like a quiet thesis statement on what Nishio matcha can be. The walk in through the garden sets the tone, and once you sit down the room is calm, unhurried, and focused on the tea and sweets rather than décor tricks. The matcha itself is rich and clear, with a bitterness that reads as depth rather than harshness. Soft serve, parfaits, and anmitsu all carry that same through line, so nothing tastes like a generic “green tea” dessert.

name: Yakiman
description: Local specialty: The eels come straight from Isshiki farms — thick, fresh, and fatty. Most diners recommend shirayaki (plain grilled) with condiments like lemon or umeboshi over the usual kabayaki sauce.

name: Omen Ginkaku-ji
description:
Omen near Ginkaku-ji is a Kyoto classic — the kind of place where the atmosphere, service, and tradition make the visit as memorable as the food. The udon noodles are fresh, silky, and pair beautifully with the light, flavorful broth and seasonal vegetables. Tempura here is crisp and not oily, and the mackerel sushi is a standout side dish.

That said, it’s very popular, so be prepared to wait, especially around lunchtime.

name: Soma Cafe
description: A legitimately good stop if you want dessert or a proper coffee break while moving through Kiso-Fukushima. The place is a renovated old house, shoes off at the door, with a small gallery on the second floor selling local woodwork and ceramics. The staff actually speaks enough English to make ordering simple.

name: ラ・メゾン・アンシェンヌ
description: Opened 2015 in a 1920s farmhouse that previously processed silkworm cocoons. Chef Masato trained at L'Atelier de Joel Robuchon Tokyo (2004-2009) before returning to his home prefecture. The menu uses ingredients within 50km radius: Hokuto city pork, Oshino village dairy, Koshu city vegetables. Wine list emphasizes Yamanashi producers including rare bottlings from Marufuji and Chateau Mercian. Dinner service only, 18:00-21:00, reservation required 3 days advance. No a la carte; set menus at 8,000, 12,000, or 18,000 yen. The building's "ancienne" designation refers to its registered status as tangible cultural property.

name: AZUMAYA Honten
description: Founded 1963. Headquarter location in Morioka. Wanko soba: small bowls (one mouthful, approximately 15g noodles) served continuously until customer places lid on bowl. 15 bowls = 1 standard portion. Servers chant "Hai don don" while refilling. Deluxe course (3,520 yen) includes toppings: tuna sashimi, nameko mushrooms, minced chicken, sesame paste, nori, pickles, grated taro, leeks, wasabi. 100+ bowls earns wooden plaque and certificate. Average consumption 30-50 bowls. Owner Akihiko Baba lived in New York 1990s; speaks English. Multiple locations; main shop near Morioka Station.

name: Akai Ringo
description: Aomori shop specializing in red-flesh apples. Varieties: Nagafu 2, Red Gold, Shinsei. Products: fresh apples, juice, wine, jam, pastries. Red-flesh apples developed in Aomori 1980s; anthocyanin content creates tart, vivid flavor. Used by world pastry chefs for color and acidity. Tasting available. Location near Tachineputa Museum.

name: Jingisukan Yamaka Susukino
description: Yamaka offers authentic Sapporo-style jingisukan in a refined setting distinct from tourist-oriented beer halls. The charcoal grilling, whole-carcass sourcing, and sauce-to-ramen progression demonstrate technical seriousness. The pawnshop warehouse atmosphere and local clientele provide cultural authenticity.

name: Senbonto Shrine
description: Nezu Shrine is where Tokyo finally shuts up for a minute. Turtles in the pond, koi cruising under that red bridge, a little tunnel of torii, and then the hillside that just erupts in azaleas late April–early May if you pay to go into the garden. Most of the year it’s just a calm neighborhood shrine between Ueno and Todai, with locals actually praying, a few food stalls on busy days, and almost none of the circus you get at Sensō-ji or Meiji.

name: DAWN | Avatar Robot Cafe ver.β
description:
DAWN isn’t a robot show. It’s a workaround for a society that still shuts people out. The pilots aren’t mascots. They’re people who want to work, earn money, and talk to customers but can’t physically show up in a building. The robots are the access ramp.

So when you sit there and a small white OriHime rolls up to your table, the point isn’t “look at the cute robot.” It’s the fact that someone at home, maybe in bed, maybe dealing with a condition that makes normal employment impossible, is still in the room with you. You’re not watching tech replace a worker. You’re watching tech give someone their job back.

name: teamLab Borderless: MORI Building DIGITAL ART MUSEUM
The National Museum of Emerging Science and Innovation (Miraikan)
description: If you care even a little about where science and society are heading, Miraikan is worth the train out to Odaiba. It’s less a “wow, robots everywhere” theme park and more a layered conversation about climate, aging, AI, and what kind of future we’re actually building. The giant Earth sphere floating in the atrium is as striking in person as the photos suggest, but the real value is in the interactive exhibits that make you think about data, bodies, and technology rather than just pressing buttons.

name: Toshima City Tokiwaso Manga Museum
description: A small but pretty special stop if you care about manga history. The building is a full-scale reconstruction of the shabby postwar apartment where Tezuka Osamu, Fujiko Fujio, Ishinomori Shotaro and other Showa-era mangaka lived and worked in 4.5-tatami rooms, rushing pages to editors. Inside you walk through recreated rooms, shared kitchen and corridors, with exhibits on the neighborhood and the grind of weekly deadlines.

name: TOKYO BUNBUN(東京文聞)
description:
I brought my film students to Tokyo BunBun as part of our Tokyo in Film program, and it turned into one of the best experiences we have had in Tokyo. Abe-san, Tomomi-san, and the whole BunBun team are generous, skilled, and completely invested in what they do. Their samurai choreography is precise and full of life, and they take the time to teach the real mechanics of movement, timing, and intent.

We filmed a full Musashi homage with them, inspired by Vagabond, and they welcomed us into their home so we could shoot the sequence properly. I was the primary videographer, editor, sound mixer, and narrator for the project, and the actors worked with us the way professionals work with professionals. The link shows the final result:
https://www.instagram.com/p/DQfI8VQj_ic/

If you care about samurai cinema, stage combat, Japanese performance traditions, or you simply want something real and memorable in Tokyo, this is the place. Tokyo BunBun is the team I trust.

name: Naruto x Boruto park Nijigen no mori
description: As a long-time Naruto fan, this felt like walking straight into the Leaf Village. The core of the park is the mission system: stamp rallies, hand-seal challenges, and the big wooden maze that has you ducking, squatting, and hunting for clues like a genin on a real assignment. It’s more physical than it looks, so be ready for stairs, heat, and very little shade in summer. The theming is loving rather than flashy, with plenty of statues, photo spots, and small details that reward you for slowing down instead of rushing through. Ichiraku-style ramen at the top of the hill is surprisingly solid theme-park food and hits especially well after the missions. Access can be confusing the first time—using the official shuttle bus from the ferry or highway bus stop is much easier than trying to improvise with taxis—so it works best as part of a full day on Awaji Island (often paired with the Godzilla attraction).

name: Godzilla Interception Operation Awaji
description: A very specific kind of heaven for Godzilla fans. The setup is lean but focused: short intro film, the zipline run at the full-size Shin Godzilla, a shooting mission, and then a museum that walks you through the history and designs. The zipline into the mouth is ridiculous in the best way and the models in the museum feel like a love letter to the series rather than a cheap tie-in. It does take some effort to reach the park and the ticket price is not small, so it makes the most sense as part of a full day on Awaji Island with the other themed areas.

name: Awajishima Anime Park
description:
Nijigen no Mori is legitimately fun and the setting is gorgeous, but you need to understand the structure before you arrive. The park is spacious and pleasant to walk through, and then each major attraction is ticketed separately. That can get expensive fast, especially if you are trying to sample everything.

The right approach is to treat it like a menu. Choose one “big” experience you are excited about (Godzilla zipline is a common highlight), then add one smaller one and leave the rest for another visit. If you do it that way, the value makes sense and you are not stressed about rushing across the park all day.

name: Katsuoji
description: One of the best day-trips from Osaka. Quiet mountain setting, tons of daruma everywhere, and the stamp route actually makes the visit fun instead of gimmicky. Go early to avoid lines. If you’re already doing Minoh Falls, adding this temple makes the whole day much better.

name: Hello Kitty Smile
description:
Very cute Sanrio themed stop on Awaji, with lots of photo spots and a few light interactive elements. The staff are friendly and the view is excellent, and the cafe is a solid bonus.

The main caveat is value. It is not a huge facility, so if you are expecting a full theme park scale experience, you will be done quickly. Treat it as a themed photo and cafe stop, not a half day attraction, and it makes a lot more sense.

Nishio
description: "Little Kyoto"

name: Matcha Museum Saijoen WAKUWAKU
description: If you are already in Nishio for Saijoen, the Matcha Museum next door is the part that makes the visit feel complete. The guided course is about 75 minutes and reservation only, so it is not a casual walk in, but once you are inside it is quiet, focused, and surprisingly hands on.

name: Saku Island
description: 22 permanent modern art installations scattered across a quiet, rustic island. Super good for wandering with a camera.

name: Edo Wonderland Nikko Edomura
description:
Edo Wonderland Nikko Edomura is one of the strongest locations in the region if your goal is recreating Edo period scenes. The streetscapes read convincingly on camera, and there are multiple zones that give you usable depth, texture, and period detail without constant modern contamination if you frame carefully.

This is also a working theme park, so the experience depends on crowd level. Go early, and weekdays are easier for clean shots. The staff commitment to character helps the atmosphere, and the live performances add real energy even if you do not speak Japanese.

name: Boso Village
description:
Excellent set like open air museum for Edo period style scene recreation. The buildings and streets give you a lot to work with, especially if you shoot tight and pay attention to angles. Some areas are more active than others depending on the day, so check what is open if you are coming for specific workshops or demonstrations.

Worth the trip from Narita if you want period locations and good photo opportunities. Bring comfortable shoes, and avoid peak sun if you plan to shoot.

name: Kuchu Teien Observatory
description:
Kuchu Teien is worth it for one reason: Osaka looks best from above, and this building gives you the cleanest 360 view without turning it into a theme park. The escalators suspended between the two towers are the thing people remember, but the real payoff is the roof. It’s open air, windy, and you actually feel how high you are.

Go at sunset, stay until the city switches on, and ignore the heart-locks and tourist fluff. It’s one of the few places where Osaka’s scale, rivers, highways, and neon all make sense in a single frame.

name: Kashihara
description: The birth place of Street Fighter. See life sized statues, paintings, grate covers, etc., all in homage to the game that was born here.

name: The Waseda International House of Literature (The Haruki Murakami Library)
description:
The Haruki Murakami Library is one of my favorite places in Tokyo. I have visited many times and it never feels like a novelty or a tourist stop. It is a quiet, carefully designed space that understands mood, pacing, and restraint.

Murakami is one of my favorite authors, and the library reflects his work without turning it into branding. The music room playing jazz from the novels is especially well done and actually shapes how you experience the space rather than feeling decorative.

The café is good and makes it easy to stay for a long time reading or thinking. This is a place built for reflection, not crowds. Highly recommended for readers and anyone interested in literature.

name: ハネトや
description: Rental 3,000-5,000 yen for full festival period. Purchase 10,000 yen. Costume includes: flower hat with bells, yukata, obi sash, tabi socks, hand towel. Required to join parade dancing. Rental shops throughout Aomori City; A-FACTORY and Wa Rasse museum have dedicated services. No registration required; join any float group. Dance: jumping with "Rassera, rassera" chant. Physical exertion significant; 2-hour parade duration.

name: Aomori Gyosai Center (Aomori Nokkedon)
description: Morning market operating since 1950. "Nokke-don" system: buy tickets (1,300-2,000 yen for 5-10 tickets), exchange at stalls for seafood toppings over rice. 30+ stalls. Specialties: scallops, sea urchin, salmon roe, squid, local fish. Operating hours 05:00-15:00 (varies by stall). Located 5 minutes from Aomori Station. Second floor seating. Cash preferred; some stalls take IC cards.

name: Nebuta Museum WA RASSE
description: Museum opened 2011. Four full-size Nebuta floats on display (rotated annually). Floats 9m long, 5m wide, 7m high. Paper-pasting workshops available (reservation required). Haneto costume try-on included in admission. Admission 620 yen. Open 09:00-19:00 (summer). Located waterfront, 10 minutes from station. Gift shop sells float-related merchandise.

name: BnA_WALL - Art Hotel in Tokyo
description: Staying here feels less like a standard hotel and more like sleeping inside a piece of installation art. Each room is a completely different concept, but underneath the design the basics are solid: comfortable bed, very clean space, strong in-room Wi-Fi, and a surprisingly good shower and bathroom for a compact Tokyo room. The neighborhood is quiet but central enough that you can reach most parts of the city easily by subway, and coming back here at night feels like stepping off the grid a bit.

name: Minshuku Murou
description: The house is a beautifully renovated old kominka on a hill, with big windows looking out over tiled roofs, rice fields, and Mt. Muro—on a misty morning it really does feel like the “dragon” landscape locals talk about. Meals are vegetable-forward, seasonal, and clearly cooked with care; it’s the kind of food that makes sense because you’re in the countryside, not in spite of it. The baths are simple but relaxing, the rooms are spotless and calm, and the owners are kind in a very grounded, non-hotel way—happy to pick you up, talk about the area, and help you plan a visit to Muro-ji or the dragon god spots.

name: Daikichi
description:
Daikichi is exactly what you want at the end of a Nakasendo walking day. It sits just off the main street in Tsumago, quiet once the day trippers leave, and feels like staying in a family home that has been refined over decades. The rooms are simple and clean, with thick futons and views that remind you you are in the mountains, not on a tourist circuit. The shared hinoki bath is small but genuinely relaxing after the trail.

The real reason to stay here is the hospitality and the food. The hosts are attentive without fuss, and the meals are careful, local, and just adventurous enough to remind you you are in the countryside rather than in a hotel dining room.

name: ZEN&BED 望月庵
description: Operating since 2018 in a former monk's residence built 1847. The building survived the 1923 Kanto earthquake and WWII air raids that destroyed much of Koshu. Five guest rooms, shared baths, no private toilets in original rooms (newer annex has ensuite). Morning zazen is optional; the abbot leads sessions when at least three guests participate. Breakfast is shojin ryori using vegetables from the temple's 1-hectare field. The name "Bogetsuan" refers to a 13th-century Chinese monk's hermitage. Booking through Japanese-language website only; limited English spoken.

name: STAY366
description: Built 2019 on the site of a 1980s holiday cottage. The address 366 Yamanaka gave the property its name. Architect: Hitoshi Saruta of CUBO design, known for concrete structures that frame natural views. Eight rooms, all with Fuji-facing windows, minimum 2-night stay on weekends. The lake-view rooms cost 40% more than garden-view, though Fuji is visible from both. Breakfast uses eggs from the owners' chicken coop and bread from a Koshu bakery. No restaurant; dinner requires driving 15 minutes to Yamanakako village or ordering delivery from three local options. The "epic view" depends entirely on weather; November-February offers 60% clear-sky probability, July-September drops to 20%.

name: Meiji Jingu
description:
Huge Shinto shrine complex in the middle of the city, wrapped in a forest that actually feels separate from Tokyo once you pass the giant torii. The long gravel approach is the point: quiet, tree-lined, and a reset after Shibuya and Harajuku, even though it can still be crowded. The main shrine is simple and spacious rather than ornate, with wedding processions and children in formal dress common on weekends. Entrance to the grounds is free; the Inner Garden and treasure museum charge small separate fees and are worth it if you want more time in nature, a lily pond, and a bit of sword and Meiji history.

name: Fukagawa Fudou-dō (Naritasan Tokyo branch temple)
description:
If you only have time for one temple experience in Tokyo, make it this one. The main hall is a modern concrete space, but the goma fire ceremony is intense and unforgettable: monks chanting, taiko drums shaking the floor, conch shells, and columns of flame rising in front of Fudō Myōō. Services run several times a day, and it is worth sitting through the full ritual. Take off your shoes, keep your phone put away, and just let the sound and smoke wash over you.

The ferris wheel gives a clear view of the bay, and the bird sanctuary is worth the walk if you want something calmer than the aquarium. Bring what you need before you enter because food options inside the park are limited.

name: Kumano Hongu Taisha
description:
Kumano Hongū Taisha is located in the centre of the Kii Mountains, at the confluence of the Kumano and Otonashi Rivers. Its original entrance is marked by the world's largest shrine gate (called Torii) - the Ōyu no hara Torii - which is 34 metres high and 42 metres wide. Being destroyed by floods (and rebuilt) a few times in its history, Kumano Hongū Taisha was relocated from its original position by the Kumano River to higher ground nearby in 1889. Among others, Kumano Hongū Taisha enshrines Izanagi, the founding father deity of Japan.

name: Kumano Hayatama Taisha
description:
Kumano Hayatama Taisha is located on the east coast of the Kii Peninsula, in Shingū City near the mouth of the Kumano River. The Grand Shrine is home to a sacred 850-year-old Podocarp tree, called Nagi no Ki. It is said that Izanagi and Izanami, the mythological couple that created Japan, first arrived in the area on a rock named Gotobiki Iwa. The rock marks the location of Kamikura-jinja, the original shrine, which pilgrims can reach by climbing a narrow 500-step stairway a few hundred meters south of the main complex.

name: Kumano-Nachi Taisha
description:
Kumano Nachi Taisha is uniquely positioned on the side of a mountain high above the Nachi River and next to Nachi Falls - at 133 metres, Japan's tallest single-drop waterfall and the home of Hiryū Gongen, another important Shinto deity. Nachi-san (as the sacred complex is often called), is also home to Seiganto-ji, a Temple of the Tendai School of Buddhism, and a sacred 850-year-old Camphor tree, which is said to grant wishes to worshippers who walk through its hollow trunk.

name: Ichigaya Kameoka Hachimangu
description:
Ichigaya Kameoka Hachiman Shrine is a small but distinctive shrine a few minutes from Ichigaya Station. The stone steps are steep, but the grounds at the top are calm and well maintained.

The shrine is especially known for prayers and amulets related to pets, and there is a wide selection available. You will see many ema dedicated to animal health. Despite its popularity for this reason, the atmosphere remains quiet and respectful.

I have visited multiple times and always find it peaceful. A good place to stop if you want a meaningful shrine visit without leaving central Tokyo.

name: Nanzo-in Temple
description:
Built in 1899 as a subtemple of Sasaguri Shingon sect headquarters. The reclining Buddha was added in 1995 after a decade of construction. It weighs 300 tons, took 6 years to cast in bronze sections, and represents the moment of the Buddha's death/entry into nirvana. The 700 rakan statues lining the approach were carved by multiple sculptors between 1980-2010, each with distinct regional styles visible in the facial treatments. The temple actively solicited donations for each statue, which explains the variety. Not ancient. Not quiet. But the scale creates genuine impact when you turn the final corner.

name: Sakurai Futamigaura's Couple Stones
description:
The "married couple rocks" (meoto iwa) are a Shinto fertility symbol found at multiple Japanese beaches. This pair was designated a national scenic spot in 1934. The white torii was added in the 1970s as a tourism draw, replacing earlier wooden structures that rotted in sea spray. The sunset view works because the rocks align roughly west-southwest. Best light occurs October-February when atmospheric clarity peaks. The beach is basalt shingle, uncomfortable for walking. Local restaurants serve squid caught offshore.

name: Bodaitei Steps
description:
Built 1632 by local lord Naito Masanaga to improve access to Kuon-ji. The 287 steps align with Buddhist numerology: 2 (harmony), 8 (prosperity), 7 (completion). Original granite was quarried locally; repairs in 1987 replaced worn treads with matching stone. The cedar canopy dates to a 1920s reforestation project—original trees were logged for temple construction and castle-building in the 16th century. Average climb time: 12 minutes at moderate pace. Heart rate peaks at step 180 where grade steepens. No railings; wear shoes with grip.

name: Hirosaki Castle
description:
Built 1611, current keep rebuilt 1810 after 1627 lightning fire. One of 12 original Edo-period keeps remaining in Japan. Only surviving keep in Tohoku. Three stories, copper-tile roofing (unique to snowy regions). Five gates and three turrets also original. Keep temporarily relocated 2015-2025 for stone wall repair; returns to original position 2025. Hirosaki Park: 2,600 cherry trees, 50 varieties, one of Japan's top three cherry blossom spots.

name: Nishio City Iwase Archives
description: Nishio City Iwase Archives is one of those places you only understand once you walk through the door. It looks small from the outside, but inside is a concentrated, carefully kept collection that feels impossible to find anywhere else. Edo-period books, early prints, publishing materials, and facsimiles you can actually handle are all presented without fuss or theatrical staging. It is quiet, serious, and incredibly well maintained.

name: Mikawakogei Glass Museum
description: Mikawakogei Glass Museum is small, tucked into a quiet residential area, and more like stepping into an artist’s house than a formal museum. Once you are inside, it works. The stained glass pieces and glass objects have a handmade, personal feel, and the big draw is the kaleidoscope spaces.

name: Jazz & Soul Bar - The Deep
description: Tiny room, grand piano, and you are close enough to hear the singers breathe between phrases. This feels less like a club and more like being invited into someone’s living room to sit with the band. I came for one set and stayed for the second, sipping whiskey and watching the pianist and vocalist trade energy at arm’s length. Staff and regulars were kind even with my clumsy Japanese, and the music charge felt more than fair for that level of playing.

name: Mandarake Complex
description: Mandarake Complex is Akihabara in concentrated form: eight packed floors of second-hand manga, figures, gunpla, trading cards, retro games, doujinshi, and every flavor of niche collectible. Stock turns over constantly, so it is the kind of place you can revisit and still stumble onto rare or out-of-print items, from Macross mecha and Digimon merch to vintage model kits and “spicy” adult floors tucked higher up.

name: AKIHABARA KOTOBUKIYA
description: Kotobukiya is the polished, curated counterpoint to Akihabara’s chaos. Instead of dusty bins and mystery shelves, you get a bright, well laid out multi-floor shop where everything is grouped by series and medium: JRPG merch, Monster Hunter, Final Fantasy, Zelda, Ghibli, Persona, Tales, VTuber floors devoted to Hololive and Nijisanji, plus a serious spread of figures and plastic model kits. It is all new stock rather than second hand, so you are paying for condition and presentation rather than gambling on thrift.

name: Akihabara Radio Kaikan
description: Ten floors of pure Akiba chaos. Figures, cards, model kits, gacha, and every kind of hobby shop stacked on top of each other. Crowded, cramped, and completely part of the fun. Prices jump around depending on the floor, so look before you buy, but if you want to understand why people come to Akihabara in the first place, this building explains it in one hit.

name: TAMASHII NATIONS STORE TOKYO
description: Small, clean, and set up like a showroom more than a shop. The displays are the real draw here. Gundam, Kamen Rider, Dragon Ball, Saint Seiya, Metal Build, all staged in museum-level setups. Stock is limited and some of the big releases sell out fast, so temper your expectations. Still, if you are already in Akihabara, this is one of the best places to see the newest Bandai figures up close before you decide what to hunt for elsewhere.

name: Blue Note Tokyo
description:
Blue Note Tokyo is one of the few places that really lives up to its reputation. The room is intimate, the sound is precise without being harsh, and every seat feels designed around the stage rather than the other way around. It is closer to a small theatre than a bar, which suits the level of musicians they bring through here.

Service is efficient and professional, from the foyer check-in to the last drink. The staff handle a full house without breaking the atmosphere, and the whole operation feels rehearsed in a good way. The food is fine but not the reason to come.

name: Mandarake Shibuya
description: Mandarake Shibuya feels less like a shop and more like an underground archive. You descend into a basement that looks and smells like a dungeon, then realize it just keeps going: aisles packed with used manga, vintage toys, figures, CDs, doujinshi, and all kinds of pop-culture relics. The layout is tight and can get warm and crowded, so it is not a casual browse; you have to be willing to take your time and dig. Prices are not always “bargain bin,” but the strength of this place is depth and weirdness rather than discounts.

name: Toy Sapiens
description: Flagship Hot Toys store that feels closer to a small museum than a shop. Floor is packed with Marvel and Star Wars sixth-scale figures, life-size statues, and beautifully lit display cases that are fun even if you never buy a thing. The downside is that most of the “wow” pieces are sold out, and DC or comics-based figures are thin compared to the movie lines.

name: Himuka Shokudo
description:
Shokudo (食堂, shokudō) are casual restaurants or cafeterias that serve a variety of inexpensive Japanese dishes. Many of them are mom-and-pop, hole-in-the-wall type restaurants where the locals eat. They are numerous across Japan in urban centers and on the countryside. 

A meal at a shokudo usually cost around 800 to 1500 yen.

name: Suzukien Asakusa
description: the world's richest matcha gelato with seven intensity levels, catering to matcha newcomers and aficionados. Established through a collaboration between Suzukien, a historic tea shop from 1853, and Nanaya, a matcha sweets factory, this venue is a must-visit for its unique range of matcha gelato flavors.

name: Tesshin
description: teppanyaki, particularly featuring premium Kuroge Wagyu beef. Their signature dish is the Kuroge Wagyu Steak, priced at 1,380 JPY plus tax, seasoned with salt, kombu, and wasabi, offering a quintessential Japanese flavor profile.

name: Yakiniku King
description: A top-rated all-you-can-eat Yakiniku restaurant in Tokyo, Yakiniku King specializes in Japanese BBQ and offers a wide selection of meats for grilling. It's known for its quality, variety, and value, making it a must-visit for meat lovers. In 2022, it beat other well-known chains like Gyu-Kaku to rank as the number one Yakiniku spot. The restaurant also caters to tourists with English touchscreen menus.

name: Fruits Parlor Gotō
description: —café with sweet fruit parfaits near the old Hanayashiki amusement park. The menu, which changes seasonally, features delights such as grape and melon parfaits during summer, alongside other sweets like pancakes, kakigori shaved ice, and ice cream. It's a perfect spot for those seeking seasonal fruit desserts.

name: Buta-Daigaku Shimbashi
description: —Known for its pork bowls, which cost approximately 600 Yen for a small size, this is a must-visit for savory pork bowl lovers. It is located near Shibuya.

name: Ginza Kagari - Soba
description: — (Prepare to wait) famous for its sophisticated take on chicken ramen. The restaurant's signature dish, tori-paitan, features a creamy, rich broth derived from chicken, which provides a velvety texture and deep flavor.

name: Hobo Shinjuku Norengai
description: located a short 6-minute walk from Odakyu Shinjuku Station or Minami-Shinjuku Station, offers a collection of restaurants housed in traditional Japanese houses. This area provides a more classic and atmospheric dining experience compared to the modern establishments around Shinjuku Station. The term "Noren-gai" translates to "shop curtain town close to Shinjuku," referring to the traditional curtain (noren) that signifies an open shop. These 8 renovated old folk houses host a variety of dining options, not limited to Japanese cuisine.

name: Soba House Konjiki-Hototogisu
description: —(Prepare to wait) a ramen restaurant in Shinjuku, Tokyo, celebrated for its unique and sophisticated flavors. Awarded a Michelin star in 2018, this ramen establishment is renowned for its shoyu soba.

name: Ramen Sugimoto
description: —(Prepare to wait) ramen shop located in Nakano, Tokyo. This shop offers a unique ramen experience that both locals and visitors highly praise. The restaurant is known for its special shio (salt) ramen, which includes a generous topping of chashu pork, a perfectly cooked egg, and homemade wontons.

name: Shiro-Hige’s Cream Puff Factory
description: Nestled in Setagaya, this unique spot Offers Totoro-shaped cream puffs starting at 400 Yen. It is also a spot for Studio Ghibli fans and sweet tooth indulgers.

name: Yakumo Saryō
description: This serene and minimalist setting for a traditional Japanese breakfast was designed by the renowned architect Shinichiro Ogata. It provides a genuine cultural experience through its dining, highlighting Japanese cuisine as an art form involving various cultural elements, from the dishware to the chef’s etiquette. Yakumo Saryo offers a traditional Japanese breakfast called "Asacha," focusing on tea, priced at ¥4,000 (around $37).

name: Hakushū Teppanyaki
description: This establishment shines with its premium Japanese Wagyu Beef prepared teppanyaki-style in Shibuya. It is celebrated for top-notch Kobe beef.

name: Kicks Cafe&Bar
description: A great local place to get a burger.

name: YAKITORI Nonotori Nihonbashi
description: Yakitori Nonotori in Nihonbashi offers an exceptional dining experience, particularly through its Premium Omakase Course, which features seasonal, expertly grilled skewers and side dishes. The restaurant is praised for its use of binchotan charcoal, which imparts a unique flavor to the yakitori, and its signature tamago kake gohan (rice with eggs cooked in an earthenware pot). Many diners appreciate the combination of traditional techniques with creative, modern twists, along with the attentive service. For a full experience, the omakase paired with sake or wine is highly recommended.

name: Hinoya Curry Akihabara
description: A good introduction to Japanese curry; it is a little spicy.

name: HIGUMA Doughnuts
description: HIGUMA Doughnuts in Tokyo Dome City offers fluffy, delicious donuts that are highly praised for their light texture and gentle sweetness.

name: LATTE ART MANIA TOKYO
description: If you're looking for a cool, creative coffee spot, Latte Art Mania is definitely worth a visit. I appreciated the attention to detail in their intricate latte designs. The space is small, but the energy is inviting, and the charcoal latte offers something unique—both in flavor and presentation.

name: Kantan-na Yume
description: Kantan-na Yume feels like a hidden gem tucked away in a quiet part of the city. When I visited, the peaceful atmosphere struck me right away—a nice change from the buzz of Shibuya just minutes away. The wagashi I tried were exquisite, beautifully made, and paired perfectly with a cup of matcha.

name: Homemade Ramen 麦苗
description: f you're looking for an outstanding ramen experience, I highly recommend Homemade Ramen 麦苗. I visited recently, and despite not typically favoring shoyu broths, their version completely won me over with its depth and rich umami flavor. The noodles and toppings were exceptional—the steak in the deluxe toppings was some of the best I've had. Do note that you'll need to arrive early, around 9 or 10 AM, to put your name on the list due to its popularity. But trust me, the wait is worth it.

The 1st Ward is where the CCG Main Office is located, and it serves as the headquarters for anti-Ghoul operations. It’s based on Chiyoda, home to major governmental buildings and Tokyo Station.
Notable Spot: Tokyo Station, a historic station with modern vibes, representing the CCG's power and influence.

description:
Description: The 3rd Ward features Roppongi, a famous nightlife district and key location in Tokyo Ghoul where Kaneki and Rize go on their fateful date.
Notable Spot: Roppongi Hills, known for its luxury shopping and skyline views, including a perfect view of Tokyo Tower at night.

name: Tokyo Skytree (6th Ward)
description:
Description: In Tokyo Ghoul, the 6th Ward is known for its high-tech vibe, which is mirrored by Taitō’s Tokyo Skytree, the tallest tower in Japan, representing a modern and futuristic Tokyo.
Notable Spot: Tokyo Skytree — a great spot for viewing Tokyo’s cityscape and tying in the "Neo-Tokyo" feel.

name: Tokyo Metropolitan Government Building (JJK)
description: Description: This towering building, located in Shinjuku, appears in Jujutsu Kaisen and is an iconic structure in Tokyo. It’s featured when major city-wide incidents unfold in the series.

name: Aoyama Cemetery (JJK)

name: Hotel Gajoen Tokyo (Sprited Away)
description: Hotel Gajoen in Tokyo is believed to have inspired the design of the bathhouse in Spirited Away. Known as one of Tokyo's "Museum Hotels," the hotel features stunning, traditional Japanese architecture with lavish interior designs, ornate rooms, and unique artistic displays, closely resembling the detailed design of the bathhouse in the film.

name: NTV Big Clock designed by Hayao Miyazaki

name: Kanda Yabu Soba
description: a favorite of mine; a soba restaurant renowned for its traditional Edo-style noodles. The restaurant, rebuilt following a fire, continues to serve various soba dishes, including the Kamo-san ban soba featuring thick slices of duck and the ten-seiro soba paired with crispy shrimp.

name: KEY'S CAFÉ 秋葉原SEEKBASE店
description: A coffee shop within walking distance in Akihabara with wifi and good group seating. Open early and is a good place to study.

name: KOMEDA'S Coffee
description: This nearby coffee shop is open early, offers good breakfast deals, and has spacious booths for group work or studying. It is a great place to get out of the hostel in the morning.

name: Karashibi Miso Ramen Kikanbō Kanda Honten
description:
—(Prepare to wait) popular for its intensely spicy Karashibi Miso Ramen. The interior, characterized by its black paint, taiko music, and festival-style devil masks, adds to the immersive dining experience. You can customize their spice level on a scale of five for both "kara" (chili heat) and "Shibi" (numbing spice from sansho pepper mix), catering to varying spice tolerances.
1. Feel free to challenge my “Oni” title; we can sit side by side if you live that spicy life. 😉

name: Himuka Shokudo
description:
Shokudo (食堂, shokudō) are casual restaurants or cafeterias that serve a variety of inexpensive Japanese dishes. Many of them are mom-and-pop, hole-in-the-wall type restaurants where the locals eat. They are numerous across Japan in urban centers and on the countryside. 

A meal at a shokudo usually cost around 800 to 1500 yen.

name: SUSHIRO Ueno
description: Many sushi plates at Sushiro are priced at just ¥100, making It an affordable and popular option for conveyor belt sushi in Tokyo.

name: Suzukien Asakusa
description: the world's richest matcha gelato with seven intensity levels, catering to matcha newcomers and aficionados. Established through a collaboration between Suzukien, a historic tea shop from 1853, and Nanaya, a matcha sweets factory, this venue is a must-visit for its unique range of matcha gelato flavors.

name: Syabu-Yō
description: An all-you-can-eat shabu-shabu haven starting from 1,539 Yen for weekday lunch, located on the 4th floor of Atre Akihabara 2, directly accessible from Akihabara Station's Showa-Dori Gate. The restaurant utilizes a touchscreen ordering system in English, Chinese, or Korean, catering efficiently to tourists.

name: Tesshin
description: teppanyaki, particularly featuring premium Kuroge Wagyu beef. Their signature dish is the Kuroge Wagyu Steak, priced at 1,380 JPY plus tax, seasoned with salt, kombu, and wasabi, offering a quintessential Japanese flavor profile.

name: Yakiniku King
description: A top-rated all-you-can-eat Yakiniku restaurant in Tokyo, Yakiniku King specializes in Japanese BBQ and offers a wide selection of meats for grilling. It's known for its quality, variety, and value, making it a must-visit for meat lovers. In 2022, it beat other well-known chains like Gyu-Kaku to rank as the number one Yakiniku spot. The restaurant also caters to tourists with English touchscreen menus.

name: Fruits Parlor Gotō
description: —café with sweet fruit parfaits near the old Hanayashiki amusement park. The menu, which changes seasonally, features delights such as grape and melon parfaits during summer, alongside other sweets like pancakes, kakigori shaved ice, and ice cream. It's a perfect spot for those seeking seasonal fruit desserts.

name: Buta-Daigaku Shimbashi
description: —Known for its pork bowls, which cost approximately 600 Yen for a small size, this is a must-visit for savory pork bowl lovers. It is located near Shibuya.

name: Ginza Kagari - Soba
description: — (Prepare to wait) famous for its sophisticated take on chicken ramen. The restaurant's signature dish, tori-paitan, features a creamy, rich broth derived from chicken, which provides a velvety texture and deep flavor.

name: Hobo Shinjuku Norengai
description: located a short 6-minute walk from Odakyu Shinjuku Station or Minami-Shinjuku Station, offers a collection of restaurants housed in traditional Japanese houses. This area provides a more classic and atmospheric dining experience compared to the modern establishments around Shinjuku Station. The term "Noren-gai" translates to "shop curtain town close to Shinjuku," referring to the traditional curtain (noren) that signifies an open shop. These 8 renovated old folk houses host a variety of dining options, not limited to Japanese cuisine.

name: Soba House Konjiki-Hototogisu
description: —(Prepare to wait) a ramen restaurant in Shinjuku, Tokyo, celebrated for its unique and sophisticated flavors. Awarded a Michelin star in 2018, this ramen establishment is renowned for its shoyu soba.

name: Ramen Sugimoto
description: —(Prepare to wait) ramen shop located in Nakano, Tokyo. This shop offers a unique ramen experience that both locals and visitors highly praise. The restaurant is known for its special shio (salt) ramen, which includes a generous topping of chashu pork, a perfectly cooked egg, and homemade wontons.

name: Shiro-Hige’s Cream Puff Factory
description: Nestled in Setagaya, this unique spot Offers Totoro-shaped cream puffs starting at 400 Yen. It is also a spot for Studio Ghibli fans and sweet tooth indulgers.

name: Yakumo Saryō
description: This serene and minimalist setting for a traditional Japanese breakfast was designed by the renowned architect Shinichiro Ogata. It provides a genuine cultural experience through its dining, highlighting Japanese cuisine as an art form involving various cultural elements, from the dishware to the chef’s etiquette. Yakumo Saryo offers a traditional Japanese breakfast called "Asacha," focusing on tea, priced at ¥4,000 (around $37).

name: Hakushū Teppanyaki
description: This establishment shines with its premium Japanese Wagyu Beef prepared teppanyaki-style in Shibuya. It is celebrated for top-notch Kobe beef.

name: Summit
description: A local grocery story with fresh takeaway choices and sales.

name: Yatai Hamachan
description: Affordable seafood and izakaya-style dining, famous for its fresh fish and sashimi. Sashimi three kinds at 950 YEN (about $7.10)

name: Niku no Ohyama
description: Known for its deep-fried delights, including beef and seafood, with varying prices based on ingredients.

name: Sanzoku Kaizoku
description: known for Takoyaki and Kaisendon, the latter being exceptionally good with various fish trimmings on rice.

name: YAKITORI Nonotori Nihonbashi
description: Yakitori Nonotori in Nihonbashi offers an exceptional dining experience, particularly through its Premium Omakase Course, which features seasonal, expertly grilled skewers and side dishes. The restaurant is praised for its use of binchotan charcoal, which imparts a unique flavor to the yakitori, and its signature tamago kake gohan (rice with eggs cooked in an earthenware pot).

name: Hinoya Curry Akihabara
description: A good introduction to Japanese curry; it is a little spicy.

name: da GIORGIO
description: Brick oven style pizza.

name: HIGUMA Doughnuts
description: HIGUMA Doughnuts in Tokyo Dome City offers fluffy, delicious donuts that are highly praised for their light texture and gentle sweetness.

name: LATTE ART MANIA TOKYO
description: If you're looking for a cool, creative coffee spot, Latte Art Mania is definitely worth a visit. I appreciated the attention to detail in their intricate latte designs. The space is small, but the energy is inviting, and the charcoal latte offers something unique—both in flavor and presentation.

name: Kantan-na Yume
description: Kantan-na Yume feels like a hidden gem tucked away in a quiet part of the city. When I visited, the peaceful atmosphere struck me right away—a nice change from the buzz of Shibuya just minutes away. The wagashi I tried were exquisite, beautifully made, and paired perfectly with a cup of matcha.

name: Homemade Ramen 麦苗
description: f you're looking for an outstanding ramen experience, I highly recommend Homemade Ramen 麦苗. I visited recently, and despite not typically favoring shoyu broths, their version completely won me over with its depth and rich umami flavor. The noodles and toppings were exceptional—the steak in the deluxe toppings was some of the best I've had. Do note that you'll need to arrive early, around 9 or 10 AM, to put your name on the list due to its popularity. But trust me, the wait is worth it.

name: Udatsu Sushi
description: Some of the best Sushi I have ever experienced. Check the prices first.

name: Menya Nishikawa
description: Beef ramen that might change your life.

name: tonkatsu.jp Omotesando
description: Pork that is on a entirely different level.

name: Torisawa 22
description: Yakitori on another level; huge wait lsit.

name: Men Mitsui
description: If you're in Asakusa and craving top-tier ramen, Men Mitsui is a must-visit! This renowned spot near Tawaramachi Station offers an incredible soy sauce ramen with medium-thick, hand-kneaded noodles, which soak up the rich yet elegantly balanced chicken and seafood broth. The char siu is exceptional, with both thick and seared belly cuts that deliver juicy, flavorful bites, and the side options like the char siu rice bowl and homemade sauce katsudon add an extra touch of indulgence. With its relaxed, traditional atmosphere, flexible ticketing system, and thoughtful service, Men Mitsui truly earns its place as one of Tokyo's standout ramen destinations.

name: Ramenya Shima
description: Ramen-ya Shima in Nishi-Shinjuku delivers an extraordinary ramen experience that’s worth every bit of effort to secure a reservation. The rich soy sauce broth has a sharpness and depth that’s perfectly complemented by tender, thin noodles, while the toppings—from soft char siu to runny-yolk eggs—add layers of texture and flavor. Both the soy sauce and salt ramen options are outstanding, with the salt version bringing a subtle, savory punch that lingers beautifully. Paired with the grilled char siu rice, this bowl of ramen stands among Japan's best, making each visit a blissful culinary highlight.

name: Kibun Sushi
description: If you’re looking for top-quality Edomae sushi in Asakusa, Kibun-zushi is a classic spot with over a century of history and a well-earned reputation. Reservations are essential; on my visit, every seat at the counter was filled, mostly with regulars. The atmosphere inside is dim and quiet, with no curtain on the entrance, creating a low-key vibe.
